utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. All the accused are here. If there are problems with interpretation, please as usual let us know. All the Defence teams are present, minus Mr. Bourgon, as previously explained. Prosecution, Mr. Nicholls and Mr. McCloskey. The witness is present in court as I speak. Are there any preliminaries? I suppose none. Remind me when this witness finishes, I need to communicate something to you in relation to your motion on protective measures. So where were we? I understand -- I understand, I've been told that Mr. Krgovic and Mr. Sarapa would like to cross-examine the witness as well. Is that -- is my information correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Very few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So Mr. Lazarevic, we had cut you short yesterday before you had finished your cross-examination. Good morning to you, sir. Witness, I'm speaking to you. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you had a good rest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pretty good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And as I told you you'll be sitting on that chair for about another hour after which you'll be free to go. Mr. Lazarevic, who was cross-examining you yesterday, and he is lead counsel appearing for Accused Borovcanin, will continue his cross-examination. He will then be followed by three other Defence teams and that -- your cross-examination or your testimony will be over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Lazarevic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I think I will have just two or three questions for you and my cross-examination will be finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you kindly [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can actually read it. Okay. Go ahead, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, my questions now have to do with your arrival at Tisca, when you got there, and when the Serb soldiers turned you back. After being taken to the school at Luke, how many people were brought there after you, in front -- to the meadow in front of the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 22 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And the people were brought in throughout the entire day you were in Tisca, sometime in the morning and people were arriving throughout the day, is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that I was there at about 10.00, so after 10.00, right up until it got dark, people were continuously being brought to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Were these people who were in the buses, who had come to Tisca in the buses and then were turned back from there and brought to Luke?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. Exactly. Except for a couple of people who had told the Serbian soldiers that they had set off into the woods and that's where they were captured and then brought to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Those other 20 who you mentioned were brought to Tisca in buss and then after that were brought to Luke, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The number of people is 22. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So 20 people entered the school in Potocari and came to Tisca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Have you made up your minds who is going first? Mr. Krgovic, who is appearing for General Gvero, will now cross-examine you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to put some questions to you related to the answers you gave to my learned friend Mr. Lazarevic during his cross-examination. He asked you about - and you answered him - about your brief stay when you were in Tuzla, when you were a member of the 26th Brigade. Do you remember the 28th Brigade? 286th Brigade, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is 286th Brigade that was formed in the settlement of Stupari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said then that you joined the brigade in order to receive humanitarian aid and so that you can receive something to help you support yourself and your family. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said and I thought that was the way for me to implement my other rights by joining the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So this functioned in the way that members of the brigades would receive humanitarian aid and had priority in receiving humanitarian aid and other -- and implementing other rights?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You are mixing it up. It's not humanitarian aid. It's compensation for members of the brigade that was received over there. It was a small amount in money, there were also donors of the brigade who would donate certain articles, like food and things which the brigade then distributed to its members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So you received a kind of payment in food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The salary or the payment actually boiled down to both of those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this is how it functioned at that time, in 1995, the -- those who were members, who were in the army, would receive their payment in food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that you're misunderstanding me. This would happen occasionally, when we are talking about food, when there were donors and if they would donate something. But there was a monetary compensation involved also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But generally, that is how it functioned? This is what my question is about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It functioned like anything else. There was compensation. Just like any other compensation you would receive it after a month of work. It wasn't different from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The other thing that I wanted to ask you is that responding to Mr. Meek's questions yesterday, when you were talking about your stay in Potocari, you mentioned the people who treated you properly when addressed you and asked for your ID card. You said one of them spoke with a Montenegrin accent. You remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that and this is my opinion. It can be correct and it doesn't have to be correct. The person who spoke to me seemed to me to speak with a Montenegrin accent. However, if this is true or not, I'm not sure. All I'm saying is that that was his accent when he was speaking to me. I don't know if the other people had accents like that. I heard only one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the people who come from Herzegovina, their accent and the accent of people who come from Montenegro is similar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. I didn't really meet so many people from Herzegovina. I met more people from Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what date that was, was that on the 11th do you recall, or was it on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The 12th. You were in Potocari on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 11th in the afternoon, I got there, spent the flight there, was there on the 12th, and then early in the morning on the 13th, we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That day, on the 11th of July, when you were in Potocari, that area where you were, was it shelled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the area, but the immediate vicinity was hit by shells. I recall one shell fell so close that women and children started screaming and threw themselves on the concrete floor. You could feel that detonation quite close.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So you were outside of the base, you were in the vicinity of the UN base?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN base was a little bit closer to Bratunac and to the battery factory so it was outside of the UN base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So the shelling that you heard was not in the direction of the base but to the outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't tell you. It was about half a kilometre off, away from the base, but in any case, you could hear the sound and the feel -- feel the shaking of the detonation in that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So it wasn't in the base itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So the base wasn't shelled on that day, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The base is something else. It's in the direction of Bratunac and it's away from the place where I happened to be, so I was not at the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: All I'm asking you is if you know whether the base was shelled or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Madam Fauveau, who is appearing for General Miletic, will now cross-examine you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday you mentioned the bombing of Srebrenica. You said this happened at the end of 1992, at the beginning of 1993. Just before that, yesterday, on page 46, line 11 to 19 you described the humanitarian situation in Srebrenica. I would like to know whether the situation which you described, whether this also refers to 1993, 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think there was a mistake into B/C/S. I talked about 1992 and 1993 to begin with.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned only the end of 1992. Throughout the war in Srebrenica, there was shelling of Srebrenica. With respect to your other question, the humanitarian situation in this period, then and after the convoys began to arrive, the situation was different because the convoys began to arrive. I have to say, however, that the convoys were frequently stopped and looted in Bratunac and that only those parts of convoys were allowed to pass through that the Serbs wanted to let go. That is, soap, beans, blankets, but important staples such as salt, sugar, oil, sometimes flour, tins of food were frequently confiscated in Bratunac. Flour did sometimes did arrive but in very small amounts. If I have to say whether there was a difference, yes, there was, but the situation had not been solved because the number of people there increased tremendously in that period, and the hunger and suffering of the population were extremely evident everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you say that there was a difference, are you saying that the situation improved after the arrival of the UN?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference was there for as long as the convoys kept arriving but I said also that the convoys were stopped and looted so there wasn't really that much of a difference. It was still a catastrophe. Of course, you could see a difference when the convoys arrived regularly as planned and then when flour was distributed to the people. If there were no convoys then if they were stopped, then you just had the catastrophic situation that you had before.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that there were a lot of rumours going around Srebrenica. Did you hear anything about the abuse of humanitarian aid and smuggling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really say anything about that. There were rumours, but what -- what really -- I cannot say anything to respond to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we show the witness Exhibit number 5D31, please? This is a summary or rather a report or rather a summary provided by the Ministry of Affairs of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Srebrenica; at the time it was a protected area.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In B/C/S -- this will be on page 8 of the English version. This is a paragraph which begins with, "Besides." This is a paragraph you can see on your screen. In English this starts on page 8, paragraph 3. Sir, in this paragraph, you can read as follows: "[In English] Besides this, in conversation with expelled person from Srebrenica. We registered numerous criminal activities committed by members of the 28th Division and some leaders of Srebrenica municipal authorities which in any case influenced the stabilisation of the situation and complication of security in this enclave. Persons who were close to these categories were involved in the criminal activities and they were one of the links in the chain of smuggling of humanitarian aid, remonstrating, smuggling of fuel et cetera." [Interpretation] Sir, had you heard anything about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This for me is a ridiculous question. Madam, you must put questions to me that have to do with me personally and my statement. I'm not the person who could respond to a question like this. I wasn't involved in this sort of work and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. There are ways and ways of addressing a person. And when you are addressing Defence counsel, who is only doing her duty here, there is only one way, and that's not the way that you have addressed her. So I want you apologise to her first and foremost. And then if you are not in a position to answer her question, you just answer by saying so. But you have no right to tell Madam Fauveau or anyone else for that matter in this courtroom that that is a ridiculous question, that that question shouldn't be asked or the way you addressed Madam Fauveau. So please, let's start with a proper apology. And then you answer the question. I am here to protect you. I am here to protect also Defence counsel, Prosecutor and every single person that is working under difficult conditions in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that I did not made any -- make any mistake. I said right away that I didn't know the answer to this question, but if you believe that I need to offer an apology, then I am doing so. I think that I answered this question before by saying that I didn't know. I didn't intend any insult or anything, but there is a question pertaining to the division of humanitarian aid. I wasn't involved with that. I didn't do anything related to that. So this is what I said. I didn't mean to be provocative or insolent. I was just making it known that there was no point in going further with these questions. That was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But that's up to us to decide and not up to you, Witness. We are the Judges in this case, not you. And if there is a reason in your mind why you shouldn't answer a question, then you address yourself to us and not to counsel. And we will tell you whether to go on and answer the question or not. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so -- I believe the question has been asked and answered, in the context of rumours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it has been answered but that didn't justify the way he retorted. So yes, Madam Fauveau, your next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, have you ever heard that people were going from Srebrenica to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that people were forced to go to Zepa to get food.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we move to page 10 of the B/C/S version of this document, please? And this will be on page 12 of the English text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 12?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is right. I'm sorry, this will be on page 9 of the B/C/S text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in the English text?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is on page 12 of the English text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The paragraph which begins with number 6, which is a -- very legible on the screen. In the English version it's the last paragraph and you then need to turn over on to the next page, page 13. "[In English] About 150 persons from Srebrenica came to Zepa and bought from Stitkovac [phoen] 1150 litres of fuel at the price of 1 DM a litre and re-sold the same quantity in Srebrenica at the price of 7 to 8 DM per litre. Stitkovac was buying the fuel from the members of the Ukrainian battalion." Sir, have you ever heard about members of the UN selling some of their goods, foods -- food or other items to the people of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. We need to establish whether the witness's name appears anywhere on the face of any one of the pages of these documents. I am not in a position to see -- I don't have the B/C/S version. I have the English version. But I wouldn't imagine so because this is a government document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can reassure you his name does not appear anywhere in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we can proceed. Thank you. Sorry for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned your arrival in Potocari, you testified about the time when you tried to reach the buses. You stated that you saw that the UN soldiers were trying to prevent people from going to the buses out control. This is page 1256 of the Krstic transcript in -- on the 24th of March 2000. Can it be said that it was difficult to maintain control and order in Potocari at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we are talking about blocking the buses, they were actually just checking or controlling. When I said that people were passing without any kind of control, what I meant was that properly, two or three people, women, were passing through, in smaller groups, so that was checked. I think that this was a practice introduced by Serb soldiers because they wanted to monitor people and wanted to have people proceed to the buses more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But isn't it fair to say that in proceeding in this way, they could prevent any wounding and prevent any stampede?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it was a large number of people, a large crowd, so that was also possible. However, the truth is something else. They wanted to separate all the men, and that was the only way to do it, to have people proceed to the buses in that particular way so that it was possible to see whether it was a woman, a child or a man, and then they would get a chance to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You stated that there was a large crowd of people. Is it fair to say that everybody wanted to leave Potocari, they were in a hurry to do so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, everybody wanted to be on the free territory immediately. I can tell you that from my own experience. But this was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the Krstic case on page 1248 of the transcript on 24 March 2000 you stated you went to Potocari because if you had stayed in your house you would have been killed. And indeed, all those who stayed were killed. But isn't it fair to say that all the residents of Srebrenica left before the Serbs arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs did enter the town. They were already in the town. The Serbs from Zeleni Jadar and Kucana Basta [phoen] and Petric and in the centre, so the Serb army was already in the town and the people, of course, were afraid of the Serbian army, so they were pressed back in the direction of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But would you agree with me to say that everybody went, left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, there were people who remained. I heard from friends of mine that their relatives stayed behind and they never saw their relatives again, which means that they were killed in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we move to private session so that nobody will hear? If we were to do so would you be willing to give us the names of those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember the names of those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So there is no need to go into private session, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Still in the Krstic case, page 1251 of the transcript of the 24th of March 2000, you testified that on the 12th of July, the mere presence of Serbian soldiers would raise panic and you added that the soldiers who then appeared did behave quite decently. Is it therefore fair to say that the mere presence, the mere knowledge, that the Serbs were about to come, would cause panic among the population in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good question. When referring to the first group of Serb soldiers who entered, they behaved quite normally. This was panic but far less of panic. The Serb soldiers who entered the town the next day and separated people off and killed them in the immediate vicinity, those were two completely different groups of people. The first group only checked identities but didn't kill. The second group killed people. And of course there was panic because if you see someone being killed in your immediate vicinity or somebody comes up to you and says they saw blood on the ground, then of course panic spreads among people.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But, sir, the panic I have in mind is the one caused by the arrival of the first soldiers, because these are the ones you mentioned on pages 1250 and 1251 of the Krstic transcript, in which you stated, and I quote, "[In English] The mere presence of the Serb soldiers even though I must point out that those Serb soldiers behaved very decently." [Interpretation] This was your answer to the Prosecutor's question as to why suddenly there was panic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: My question is now, as follows, but isn't it fair to say that the mere fact that people knew that the Serbs were about to come would cause panic among the population in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb -- the Serb soldiers, when they entered, yes, it's true there was panic. What I'm saying is that the panic was greater when the second group arrived and started separating people. It's true that there was panic when the first group arrived, but they were only checking men's identities whereas the second group separated people off and killed them. Both groups caused panic, but the first group caused less panic than the second because I didn't observe the first group killing people, whereas the second group took people away and killed them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Madam Fauveau. So it's Mr. Sarapa left? Mr. Sarapa is defending General Pandurevic in this case. Mr. Sarapa -- together with Mr. Haynes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Can we move into private session for my first question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. By all means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that Srebrenica covered a small area and that rumours spread quickly. Was that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that, I was referring to the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Tell me, did rumours also spread about the actions of the Muslim forces in the surrounding area, around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to tell you that people were more interested in things that affected them personally, such as food and getting out and the war ending. People who were interested in finding certain -- finding out certain things, they did spread those rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Did you hear, between the beginning of the war until the events linked to the fall of Srebrenica, did you hear anything about the activities of the Muslim army or, rather, the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I heard -- I'm afraid I'm not the right person to answer this question because I was not a member of the army, so I couldn't really tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Yes. I know that you did not participate in those actions directly as a soldier. What I would like to know, however, is whether you heard about those actions, whether you heard stories about them in town.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, even if I did, I might give you the wrong information here because I'm not a person who can give you the proper information about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll be very specific. Did you ever hear rumours about Serb villages around Srebrenica being burnt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard about people going to find food in Serb villages. I did hear about that, people going to search for food, because they had to. They had to either starve to death or go and die on a front line around Srebrenica, or be killed by stepping on a land-mine, or to survive if they managed to get through and bring food back from a Serb village. So this was actually a struggle for survival. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted). It was a daily struggle for survival, how to survive today. And wake up tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: How did people go to get food? Did they trade with the Serbs to get food or did they rob the Serbs of food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it was women and children who went to get food without weapons, and of course if people had weapons, it's very likely that they took their weapons along, but the main aim of this was not to take territory, as far as I know, but to bring back food.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Please answer my questions. Did you ever hear that the Muslim forces burnt down a single Serb village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, your definition leads me to say that I didn't. I did hear more than once that people from Srebrenica went not to a single village but to several villages. Your definition is different. So I can't give you an answer according to your definition. I'm telling you that I heard people from -- about people from Srebrenica going to several Serb villages and bringing back food.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Well, were the people armed whether they went to get food or did they go to buy food from the Serbs or to ask the Serbs for food?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, can you be specific to a time frame? Because we are talking of a long time, long period of time, so -- and I honestly don't see the relevance at this point in time but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: In the period from the beginning of the military conflict, my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you referring to 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995? What --

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. No, yes. I am speaking of the entire time period, this entire time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So your last question on this matter and we'll move on to something different, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I'm talking about the time period in which military conflicts occurred and I want the witness to say whether he ever heard about Muslim forces burning down a Serb village and whether he knows of any such villages, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already given you my answer. You have defined this erroneously. I'm telling you that the Muslim people from Srebrenica went to Serb villages to get food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Move to the next question, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Just one more question in connection with this. Was this looting? Looting of food?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I object at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And your objection is sustained. Why do you ask him whether this was looting or not, if he has already -- first of all, he's not a lawyer. Secondly, he's not an international law expert. And secondly, even if he says no, what's in a word in any case? I mean, let's -- the Trial Chambers decide whether there was looting or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Just one more question in connection with this topic. Could the witness tell me specifically whether it was armed or unarmed Muslims who went to get this food?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours have made a ruling and he's already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has answered that question. He told you if they didn't have arms, weapons, they didn't take weapons. If they had, naturally one would expect them to have taken them with him. He's said it already so ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Sarapa. Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes of course, let's go into private session nor a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No re-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No re-examination. I don't have any questions either. So on behalf of the Trial Chamber, and also of the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony in this Srebrenica II trial. Our staff from the Victims and Witnesses Unit will extend to you all the assistance you require to facilitate your return back home and on behalf of everyone present here, we wish you -- I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you once again for your patience, and I wish to thank all those who listened to me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, let's deal straight away with the question of exhibits. Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First, well this has already been admitted, your, decision but P02210 is the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P01765 through P01767 are photographs of the Luke school. P02281 is the pseudonym sheet, which should be under seal. P02282 is the witness's sketch which should be under seal and perhaps later we can substitute one in open with a redaction as well. P02283 is a photograph of the witness which should be under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you are not tendering, I take it, P00184.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. That was one that came up but I didn't see the need. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from any of the Defence teams? None? So they are all so admitted and P02281, 2282 and 2283 will be kept, will be preserved under seal. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We would tender into evidence two documents used in cross-examination of this witness. These are 5D94 and 5D95. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any both will be under seal, because of their content, and you will give them an exhibit number because they are being tendered not by 5Dbut by 1D.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour they will be 1D5D94.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any other Defence team wishes to tender any document, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would seek to tender 5D31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection? Both as regards Mr. Zivanovic's request and Madam Fauveau's request?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Just to note though that the witness, it was never established he had any familiarity whatsoever with that document but I don't have any huge objection to it coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It may become relevant in the arguments to come, I mean, or submissions to come. So no objection from any of the Defence teams, other Defence teams either? So they are so admitted. And the Popovic documents will be under seal. Now, Mr. McCloskey, as I stated earlier, we have something to communicate to you in relation to your recent 31st October motion for protective measures for Prosecution November witnesses. It's nothing to do with Witness 40, Witness 66, 71, and 72. There is point taken and also the fact that the Defence teams do not object. We are of course also aware that the Defence teams have not objected to the rest of your motion, but we check, and upon checking annex 2 -- annex A, sorry, annex A, we encountered some problems. I will just give you one instance, and I will not proceed much further than that. If you look at Witness 69, for example, for whom you propose pseudonym PW-129, according to your annex, that person testified in either Krstic and/or Blagojevic, and he was granted a pseudonym as Witness X, and then partial closed session. We checked and it is true that in Krstic, that was the position. But he also testified in Blagojevic and in Blagojevic he testified with face distortion and also voice distortion. In that case, he was, I think, Witness P120, please check. Same may apply to some of the others. So what we would like you to do is to check properly whether the protective measure indicated in column 3 of annex A is common to both Blagojevic and Krstic or not, because it may be the case of you having to clarify this. The other thing is this: That as to 73, Witness 73, for example, you say closed session. Was that decided before the witness started giving evidence in a proper decision or was it something that came to be in the course of the testimony? In the case of partial closed session then, I cannot imagine that having been decided in writing in any of the protective measure decisions in Blagojevic or in Krstic. I would imagine that as happens in this case, in the course of the testimony there would be a specific request by either party to go into private session, and usually there is no contest, no objection there, and the Trial Chamber goes into private session. So I think we need to know exactly what you want. Have I made myself clear enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We -- you're doing an awful lot of checking on us and we appreciate that and we will get to the bottom of these issues. I can tell you for that last person you talked about, that was closed session from the beginning. In fact, all of these people are, as you know, were the -- were intercept operators, and the -- especially back in Krstic, many of them were still working in that particular branch, which is an intel branch and obviously very secretive. Many years have gone by and -- I know some of them are still working in those branches but we will double check all these issues of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Otherwise, we don't have any other problems. So if you give your attention to this, the earliest you come back to us, the better it will be. Who is the one who is starting first? I think it's Witness 40, isn't he? I think it's Witness 40 who will be coming first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. That's the person that was in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me check for sure, because, 40, yeah, 65 ter number 40. According to my records, the first of these witnesses to testify will be Witness 65 ter number 40. Now, as far as -- he is one of the five about whom -- one of the four about whom I said there are no problems. So as far as he is concerned, you have an oral decision here and now that the requested protective measures of facial distortion and pseudonym are being granted. They will be incorporated in our final written decision, but you can communicate to the witness the decision of the Trial Chamber. All right? Okay. The rest, I think, we don't need to rush but they will be incorporated in a proper written decision. We are going to bring in the next witness. I take it there are no preliminary issues. I also take it that this is going to be a full viva voce testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And in the first break, Mr. Haynes or Mr. Meek, I don't know who is responsible, if you could kindly, as -- by way of a preliminary estimate, give us an indication of how much time you think you would require for cross-examination. All right? I mean with the usual caveat you haven't heard the examination-in-chief as yet and this is going to be a full viva voce witness. All right. Thank you. Let me -- one moment. I need to find the documents of this witness. One moment, one moment, one moment. Don't we -- there is no one in the gallery, all right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. I know that this is not the first time that you're giving evidence in this Tribunal, but I might as well remind you that our rules require before you start giving evidence you make -- you enter a solemn declaration with us that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, a declaration which is very similar or almost identical to various oaths that are taken in various -- to an oath that is taken in various jurisdictions. Madam Usher has given you the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us that you will be testifying the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable. I see that you were thinking that you would find warm weather, summer, here in the Netherlands. You came here prepared with short sleeves. I hope you also brought a coat with you. Sir, you will be testifying now in chief first, and Mr. Thayer, who is one of the lawyers in the Prosecution team, will be the one to put questions to you, but before you do so, I want to put your mind at rest, that any concerns that you had about others getting to know that you are testifying here have been addressed by the Trial Chamber upon an ad hoc request by the Prosecution. The Prosecution asked on your behalf for some protective measures, and we have granted two protective measures. The first of these is hiding your identity. We will not be referring to you by your name and family name. We will be referring to you by a pseudonym, a number. You will be referred to as Prosecution Witness 127. The other protective measure that we have put in place is facial distortion. You know that these proceedings, like every other proceedings before these tribunals, are public and they are transmitted outside these four walls. You can watch them on the internet and you can watch them on TV and -- on certain channels. That would mean that if a person does -- a person's identity is not protected, others would be able not only to hear what that person is testifying, but also to see his or her face. Now, the Prosecution has asked that we hide your face and therefore we have granted the request and you will be testifying with facial distortion. I ask the technicians to focus the camera on the witness for a while and if you look at the screen in front of you, you will see how you are going to be seen, a set of squares. That's how others outside this courtroom are going to see you. That way, we are trying to secure that your identity is further protected. Now, I also must confirm to you that in granting these protective measures, the Trial Chamber has taken into consideration the fact that all the Defence teams have agreed to the Prosecution's request to grant you these protective measures. I wanted you to know that. Is that -- are these protective measures to your satisfaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think there is nothing else for me to -- except that there will be instances when we will go into private session, and that's precisely when we will be discussing issues, matters, the discussion of which will automatically reveal your identity, such as what's your father's name, where were you born, date of birth, where do you reside. In answering such questions, one would immediately identify you. So if there are going to be any such questions, for those questions and answers we will go in private session. Private session means that whatever is said remains inside these four walls, not exactly four but let's assume that they are four. All right? Mr. Thayer, he is all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you, and Your Honours, learned colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I have a --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- document to show you and I ask you without reading out loud, could you just read it to yourself and I would ask you if you can confirm with a yes or a no that your name is printed on that piece of paper under PW-127?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we see it? Yes. The document later on will be tendered and will be kept under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I would just ask you if you could to try to stay close to the microphone and when I ask you a question or when Defence counsel ask you a question or if Their Honours ask you a question I would just ask you to wait until you've heard the entire question and speak as slowly as you can. Everything is being interpreted. We don't want to miss anything you've said. Okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And witness, if you need a break at any time, please just say so, okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could go into private session for a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We are in open session, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In July of 1995, Witness, were you a member of the Bosnian Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was your father a member of that army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Yes, but on paper only.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did he have a gun?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was he active in any way that you knew of in the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about your brother? Was he a member of the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to turn your attention to early July 1995, just prior to the fall of Srebrenica. Do you recall the Bosnian Serb army's attack against the enclave during that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what form did that attack take?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We didn't get any translation or any -- didn't get any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Nor did I, Your Honour. I'll ask the question again and see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sometimes it comes in late but this time it didn't arrive at all. Did the rest of you who are following in English get anything? No. All right. So there is a technical problem that needs to be attended to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Shall I give it another go, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's try. I haven't heard anything from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Maybe the witness can repeat the answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it's solved. Can you -- Witness, can you repeat your answer? You were first asked do you recall the Bosnian Serb army's attack against the enclave in early July 1995 and you said "Yes." And then you were asked, "And what form did that attack take?" And you gave an answer but we didn't hear it, so if you could repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer was that as far as I can remember, mostly it started with the shelling of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you have any recollection as to the date that that shelling began?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: On the 7th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: June or July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: July. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how many days did that shelling last, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: For me, it went on until the 10th. The shelling was continuous, as far as I can recall. It went on day and night, without stopping.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, without revealing the location in which you were living, what if anything did you and your family do in response to the shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: When the shelling started, because of the place where I was living, and it was exposed to heavy shelling, we had to move to our relative's place, which was a bit further down, close to the bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Witness, when you refer to a bus station, where was that bus station located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: The bus station was a little bit farther off. It was further from where I was living. It was close to the secondary, high school centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would this be closer into the actual town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You could even say that it was in the very centre itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the actual date that you and your family went to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: I would like to ask you just to repeat the question. Which period do you mean exactly, when and where?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm referring to when your family was fleeing the shelling that you just testified about. Do you recall what day that was that you went into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: I think that this was on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at that time did you also observe any of your neighbours leaving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Yes. There were a lot of people concentrated in that place, and most of them left. They went away.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did they head into Srebrenica as well, or did they also head to other destinations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Mostly they went to the centre, to the place where I went, because the shelling was not so heavy there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you indicated that you stayed with some relatives while you were there. Where were --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- you physically situated during the shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: In a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Were you inside the house during the entire time you were there or were you able to get outside on occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Yes. You could go out occasionally, for a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe what it was like in Srebrenica during this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: It was a catastrophe. It was exhausting. The shelling was continuous. It would perhaps stop for ten minutes and you would think perhaps it will stop and then it would start again. You would find yourself in an unprotected area and you could see exactly where a shell would fall. It would fall on to a house, quite close. You could see the smoke. It's very difficult to describe that experience but it was horrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see we are approaching the first break and I think this would be a logical time to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break, starting from now. There are people in the gallery. 30 minutes. Oh, I see, I'm reminded it has to be a 30-minute break because of redactions that we did. There are people in the gallery so I think you need to take the usual precautions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry for the brief delay, but we were discussing out something that came to our information and maybe we'll need to come back to you later on but for the time being, I don't want to take any more minutes from this testimony. So Mr. Thayer, you're in possession of the floor. You can proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, when we left off, you had been testifying about how you and your family were in the town of Srebrenica. Do you recall at some point returning with your family to your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the 11th. Everything was quiet so we had the feeling that it was all going to stop. It all seemed so peaceful on that morning, the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: First, I went to a place called Petric, and then I went to the place where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point did you return to Srebrenica, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. That was on the 11th, when everything seemed, all those projectiles, the fear, the problems, one had the impression that morning that it was all going to end.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, sir, did something happen that changed your mind in some way such that you returned to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Well, the lull in the shelling. We thought we could go back to our place of residence. One had the impression, at least that's what it seemed like.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then what happened once you were back home where you were living?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Until 2.00, I remember everything was all right. Everything seemed so normal. And then all of a sudden, at 2.00 p.m., shelling and shooting started from Crni Guber and Zabojna. It was terrible. Suddenly, there were all these projectiles shooting from Guber. It was a disaster. As I was a bit further away from the house where we lived, I set out toward the centre of Srebrenica. There were other people going in the same direction. My family had left the house in about ten minutes, and went to the place where they had been hiding three days before.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was there a particular location in Srebrenica where you fled, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Like everybody else, we fled to a place near the petrol station in Srebrenica. That was a kind of gathering point. There were both men and women there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did this gathering point have a name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: I only know that near that place there was a place called Kazani, near the petrol station. Further on from the petrol station the place was called Kazani.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you reunite with your family during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Yes. I was with my father, my brother, my mother and my younger sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you as a family make a decision as to what to do next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Yes. My brother, my father and I decided to go in the direction of Tuzla. My mother and my sister, like all the other women and children, went in the direction of Potocari. That was when we parted, before leaving in the direction of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And why did your mother and your sister head in the direction of Potocari, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: We thought, like everybody else, that as we knew the UNPROFOR forces were there, they might not have problems or be killed by the Serb army. As we knew from the very beginning of the war what lay in store for us if we went there, we decided to go towards Tuzla, like everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, witness, in your last answer when you refer to we decided to go towards Tuzla, you're referring to the males in your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, did anyone tell you to go to Tuzla or tell your family that the women should go to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: No. We followed the crowd. The women and children were going towards Potocari, but this was not organised. We just did what most people were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You answered a couple of questions ago that the reason that you and your father and brother headed towards Tuzla was that you knew from the beginning of the war what lay in store. Just can you be clear, what were you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to that. It's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He hasn't finished the question, but what's your objection, because it's a leading question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he hasn't finished -- He hasn't even finished the question. I have in my transcript: "You answered a couple of questions ago that the reason that you and your father and brother headed towards Tuzla was that you knew from the beginning of the war what lay in store. Just can you be clear, what were you" -- and then he was interrupted. Where is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S, I heard more. But it's not in the transcript, in the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what did you hear in B/C/S? Because this we need to know obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the interpretation, I heard, you knew what lay in store. Please be clear. And counsel was preparing to put a leading question. That was my impression, listening to the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is not different from what we have in the transcript in any case. Because in the transcript, the counsel is putting to the witness that he has already in his testimony stated that he and the rest of the family knew from the beginning of the war what lay in store, and he is being asked to explain. So -- go ahead, any way. Let's proceed straight away. Finish your question, please. If you haven't finished it as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, what were you worried about, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Well, to be quite specific, not only did we decide on our own to go towards Tuzla rather than going towards Potocari, but we followed most of the people who were already on the way towards Tuzla from the place called Kazani. It never occurred to us to go to Potocari. So that's why it seems that --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, when you stated a few moments ago that you knew what was in store for us, what did you mean when you said "in store for us"? What were you afraid of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Yes. I think I understand your question now. We were afraid because of everything that had been happening from the beginning of the war, and all the shelling in Srebrenica. It was quite evident they wanted to kill us all. Evidently that was their goal. That's what I meant. When I said from the very beginning of the war, in view of everything we had gone through, the shelling four days before, the attacks, we assumed what would happen to us if we went to Potocari. We knew not just me but all the others knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you followed some other people that were heading in a direction of Tuzla. Were there women in that group, sir, at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: At that point in time, I don't think I observed many women. There were individual cases here and there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with regard to the males in that group, when you first set out, can you describe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because it's -- I don't think I observed many -- oh, I see many women. There were individual cases. Okay, that's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought I had heard him say any woman but it is many, not any.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: With respect to the males in the group, can you describe to the Trial Chamber the age range?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: For the most part, they were of all ages, boys younger than me, people aged 30, 40, up to 60. That's the people I saw in the group I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at that point, did you see any of these people armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Not at that point in time. I didn't see anyone with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you travelling on foot, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And approximately how long did you walk, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Well, approximately we went from Kazan until night fell. As far as I can recall, it was a long journey and then we continued by night. After that, I was exhausted, hungry. I had been through so much. I fell asleep at some point during the night, but I couldn't tell you what the time was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of some of the areas through which you passed during that first day and night of walking on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Yes. I remember. I heard someone in the group say we were going through Susnjari and I remember the place called Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you awoke, what time of day was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon. We had walked from Kazani until deep into the night, through Susnjari and Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So when you woke up, this would have been the 12th of July, just to be clear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Correct. It was on the 12th of July. When I woke up neither my brother nor my father were there. They had probably become separated from me, but I won't go into details because I don't remember exactly how this happened because I was so exhausted and sleepy. When I awoke, I saw other men there, but I had the impression I had ended up at the end of the column. I thought that while I had slept, many men had passed by and gone on ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you know the name of the location where you woke up to find yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Yes. When I woke up, there were other men around me and I asked, "Where are we exactly?" And one of them said we were in a place called Buljim.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was your impression, Witness, as to your location at that point in the column of men? You testified that you were at the end of the column. Were you at the very end, towards the end?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Not at the very end. I can't say we were at the very end but it was towards the end of the column because most of them had already passed us by.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at that point, Witness, were members of the column armed that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: At that point in time, I was able to move around among the men. I was looking for my father and brother. And then I did see some 50 armed men, in my estimation. I'm referring to Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you just briefly describe, sir, the types of arms or weapons that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Mostly these were automatic rifles and semi-automatic rifles, and also hunting weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, as you made your way from that location, did the column come under attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: As we moved from Buljim, from that field where I had slept, the column was attacked. They shot at the column, threw hand grenades and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Shells. They fired shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At some point, were you reunited with your father?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: When we set out from Buljim, the column was under constant attack. As we moved through the forests and over the hills, we arrived at a hill where there was a slope on one side and there were very many men there. I don't dare give you any numbers. But when we entered that group of men, when we went in among them, I found my father. When I found him, he looked ill and I asked him what had happened. He said that as they were going from Buljim, a projectile was fired and he was lifted up by the detonation, by the force of the explosion, and thrown against a tree. He was full of bruises and found it difficult to move. When I found my father, we stayed there for a while, and then at one point we heard Serbs shouting out to each other, calling out to each other, making grimaces, and then we suddenly heard a sound which was like a strong wind or a storm, and we all wondered what was happening, and this was followed by shooting, shelling, people were running every which way. I helped my father and we went straight ahead to get away from the place where we were. There was a lot of shooting, and I saw many men falling down, who had been shot. At one point, I felt heat, I don't know what it might have been, but it was something hot, and we started to flee towards the next hill. We had to wade through a small stream, a creek, and fortunately my father and I managed to get away from that area, and we were in a place some 200 or 300 metres further on. And we could hear people moaning, crying out for help. There was shooting, firing, which never stopped, and then later on we heard people moaning and -- and then we went on until it started to get dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At some point, Witness, did you find your brother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Yes. When we managed to get out of the ambush, and I think that was the first ambush after we left Buljim. After the ambush we managed to find my brother. There was a small hill there and we stayed there. There were other people there who managed to escape or they had arrived there before. So there was a group of people there, and night fell. When we got there we couldn't continue. And I remember that again, I say again, I fell asleep because I was tired and because of everything that had happened. In the morning when I woke up, this was now on the 13th of July, at one point I looked around and I saw around me half a body. Seven to ten metres away, there were massacred bodies, there was a lot of blood. At that point it was very hot, and you could feel human blood. And I threw up. I was very afraid. And then I saw a path that had been made, I think a lot of people had made the path. They had passed that way before. So I followed the path for some 500 metres or so. And in the woods again, I met a group of people. And in this group of people, I found my father and my brother. So I got there again.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I don't want to dwell too long on the scene that you saw when you woke up on the 13th, but, Witness, did you recognise anybody among the dead?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: (redacted) Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I apologise to the Chamber and the witness for not guiding him a little better with respect to that last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It happens. I mean, you can't always be watchful for everything, and mistakes are bound to be made. So don't worry about it. Provided there is always a solution, I wouldn't worry that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you described finding your father and brother again. Can you describe the location where you were reunited with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: I didn't know what that place was, what the name of it was, but in any case, from there we could see the asphalt below, from the place where we were, where I found my father and my brother again. It was a wood and a hill, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to asphalt, what are you talking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: I'm talking about the road that was stretched down below in the canyon. That's what it looked like, a canyon. It's an asphalt road, a road.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: From your position on that hill, can you tell the Trial Chamber what you saw and heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: From that position, you could hear Serbs calling over loudspeakers for us to surrender. I saw an UNPROFOR personnel carrier with blue helmets on them, so we immediately recognised that this was the UNPROFOR. At one point, when they were calling out to us, they said, "Come down, don't be afraid. UNPROFOR is here to make it possible for you to be escorted to Tuzla."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What did you decide to do then, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Well, before we saw the UNPROFOR personnel carrier, nobody even thought about surrendering. I mean, why would we escape to the woods otherwise? But after this APC, it was my impression, well, the UNPROFOR is here, I don't think that they will kill us so easily. I thought that there was some hope, because I was tired and because of all the horrible things while crossing through the woods, I had then asked my father and my brother to go with me so that we can surrender. I think they gave us two ultimatums, one was at 12.00 and then the second one at 2.00 was when we decided to go down and surrender, because the personnel carrier was constantly going up and down there, to let people know that it was UNPROFOR, to impress that upon people better.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you give the Trial Chamber some idea of the distance from the road your position was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: No. We weren't far. They didn't even need to use a loud speaker any more to call us to surrender. We could hear voices. They were calling out to us, just like that. You could hear the voice from that distance. It wasn't really that far.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So after you made the decision to surrender, sir, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Me and my brother then helped my father to go down. We needed to walk down the hill. There were some other people too. It was like a column that was going down to the asphalt.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you describe the path that you took and what you encountered along that path?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: We were coming down the hill, and there were people who had been killed lying along the path. I saw that. You went through the woods and then there was a meadow and it was all overgrown. The terrain was such that most of us actually kept to the hill in order to get down.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point did you encounter Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: No. We could see them down there at the road, the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, as you were making your way out of the woods, can you describe for the Trial Chamber when you first encountered, in person, or at a close distance, any Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: We first had to cross a creek, then there was a small incline, and there were two Serb soldiers there and they asked us if we had money or jewellery or any other valuables and if we did have that, they wanted us to hand it over to them right away. That was the first contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Witness, did you have any money or valuables with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't have anything like that with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: So then after those first two who were asking for money, there were another two on my left side, and you could already see the house that we would pass next to later. There were two asking, "Those who have money should give it here." I didn't have anything so I passed on. Then I saw, after those two, a civilian who was killed, and he was on my right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just stop you right there. You referred to a second pair of Serb soldiers who were demanding money as you got near the house. Can you describe anything about them that you recall for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: I remember that one of them was wearing ammunition belts. He was wearing bandoliers, two of them, and then on the left side, he had insignia with the coat of arms, with the four letters S on a red background. This is what I was able to notice as I was passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You referred to a dead civilian whom you passed as you neared the house. Did you see anyone else who stood out in your mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Could you be a little bit more specific? Did I see any more dead bodies or did I see anyone else? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you see any other living civilians or anyone else who stood out in your mind as you were walking from where you emerged from the woods towards the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Yes. Other than that civilian who was killed, in front of me there was a young man. I don't know if I should say his name or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can say his name in private session. So let's go in a private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday in my office, did you watch a portion of a video?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And had you seen that video previously?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And from your recollection of the events as you were emerging from the woods, do you have any idea of how that videotape was made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-127
utterances.text: Yes. I think that I forgot to tell you that. I saw a camera on my right side. So it was before we reached the house, (redacted) (redacted). It was on the right. The cameraman was on the right-hand side and I actually did happen to look at him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
